source: queens-gambit.json :: Chapter 8: The Catalan (promoted to its own opening)
intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for the Queen's Gambit complex (1.d4 d5 2.c4), built the same way as the companion Sicilian Defense Encyclopedia: for every position, the main theoretical moves, common tries you'll actually meet, sharp/gambit lines, quiet positional systems, traps, and typical mistakes. PLANNED TABLE OF CONTENTS — Chapter 1: Understanding the Queen's Gambit (foundations — structures, breaks, plans). Chapter 2: The Queen's Gambit Declined, Main Lines (Orthodox). Chapter 3: The Exchange Variation and the Minority Attack. Chapter 4: The Tartakower, Lasker, and Cambridge Springs Defenses. Chapter 5: The Queen's Gambit Accepted. Chapter 6: The Slav Defense. Chapter 7: The Semi-Slav (Meran, Botvinnik, Moscow). Chapter 8: The Catalan. Chapter 9: The Chigorin, Albin Countergambit, and Other Rare Black Tries. Chapter 10: Traps and Tactics Compendium. Chapters will be built and appended one at a time, exactly as with the Sicilian book, with every line verified move-by-move for legality and spot-checked against current theory before being added.

studies.title: Study 3.3 — The Bb4+ Check: Meeting the Most Annoying Reply

tree.commentAfter: THE MOST ANNOYING REPLY — instead of letting White develop peacefully, Black checks first, forcing the dark-squared bishop to commit before White has decided the rest of the setup. The drawback: the bishop on b4 can become a target, and after it retreats Black has spent a tempo that normal ...Be7 setups save.

The clean, classical answer — blocking with the bishop, gaining a full tempo (the b4-bishop must move again or trade), and keeping every option open: Nf3, Qc2, b3, and the e4 break all remain on the menu.

studies.title: Study 3.4 — The Classical Tarrasch Defense: The IQP Battle

tree.commentAfter: THE CLASSICAL TARRASCH — Black accepts an isolated queen's pawn (IQP) structure on principle, in exchange for free piece play, open lines, and the half-open c-file. This is one of the most principled and dynamic defenses in the whole Queen's Gambit complex, favored by Spassky, Kasparov, and Shirov at their peak. Study 1.3c covered the general IQP structure; here is how the battle actually plays out from the Catalan move order.
developing with tempo against d4 — the whole point of the Tarrasch.
pinning pressure against e7 — the standard way to harass the Tarrasch setup before Black's pieces get too active.
